title: A mirror 645 km up can’t light a patch smaller than about 6 km: the Sun isn’t a point
body: On 26 October 2026 the Guardian reported a night-lighting test near Lone Pine, California, by Reflect Orbital, a US startup that aims to launch 50,000 mirror satellites to send sunlight down at night; US regulators approved a first one, with an 18 m mirror, in July, and critics have asked them to reconsider ([the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/26/california-sunlight-space-mirrors-satellites)). Physics sets what each mirror can do. The Sun is a disc about 0.53° across ([NASA](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html)), so light from its opposite edges arrives at slightly different angles and leaves a mirror spread by the same 0.53°: the lit patch is an image of the Sun, about 6 km wide from 645 km overhead, whatever the mirror’s size. The 254 m² of sunlight on the mirror is shared over about 28 km², roughly 1/111,000 of full sunlight, or about 3.6 times the light of a full Moon, at best. A curved mirror can’t beat that: seen from the ground, a mirror can at most shine like a bit of the Sun’s surface, so its light is the share of the Sun’s disc it covers in your sky.

slides.question: An 18 m mirror 645 km up reflects sunlight onto a patch of ground. At best, how many times as bright as a full Moon?
slides.explanation: About 3.6 full Moons: the mirror’s 254 m² of sunlight spreads over about 28 km², roughly 1/111,000 of full sunlight. A full Moon is about 400,000 times dimmer than the Sun.

slides.alt: Animation on a desert night: a mirror satellite beams light down. In a side view, rays from opposite edges of the Sun spread the beam into a 6 km patch; sunny spots under a tree; a tiny mirror dot inside a huge patch; a ladder from full Moon to noon Sun; the Sun’s disc with the mirror as a speck.

slides.prompt: Change the mirror, its height and its angle. Light the patch at least as brightly as a full Moon with a mirror no wider than 8 m.
slides.takeaway: Brightness goes with (mirror width ÷ distance)²: lower the orbit to about 500 km and an 8 m mirror manages one full Moon. Wherever you put it, the patch stays an image of the Sun, kilometres wide.

slides.heading: The mirror and the patch of ground it lights, by area
slides.note: For an 18 m mirror 645 km straight overhead. At a slant the patch is bigger and dimmer.

slides.heading: Why a curved mirror can’t help
slides.text: A mirror can’t make light brighter than its source. Seen from the ground, the best any mirror can do is shine like a piece of the Sun’s surface. So the light it sends you is the share of the Sun’s disc it covers in your sky: an 18 m mirror 645 km up is about 1/333 of the Sun’s width, and (1/333)² is about 1/111,000.

slides.question: Why can’t an 18 m mirror 645 km up light a patch of ground just 18 m wide?
options: The Sun is a disc, not a point
The air bends the light apart
slides.explanation: Light from opposite edges of the Sun arrives at angles 0.53° apart, so the reflected beam spreads by 0.53°: about 6 km over 645 km.
